the hybrid small molecule 36 potently disrupts the interaction of polymerase acidic protein–basic protein 1 (PB1) subunits, and it shows anti-influenza activity in a cell-based model with no cytotoxic effects.
the hybrid compound 36, endowed with the ability to inhibit PA-PB1 interactions, is also able to inhibit the replication of the virus in cell cultures.
we identified a hybrid small molecule able to disrupt the PA-PB1 protein-protein interaction with high potency, which is a promising lead for the design of new anti-Flu drugs.

the identification of a new class of small molecules endowed with the potential to disrupt PA-PPB1 interaction, and therefore able to interfere with the RNA replication cycle of Flu.

the design of a novel series of hybrid small molecules able to interfere with the PA-PB1 protein-protein interaction, and the identification of compound 36 as one of the most potent PA-BP1 disruptors reported so far, which may represent a starting point for the development of new anti-Flu agents.

the identification of new hybrid small molecules endowed with the dual ability of disrupting PA-PB1 interactions and displaying antiviral activity against influenza virus, which may represent an interesting lead for the discovery of new antiviral agents.

the 2-amide moiety is a key structural feature for PA-PB1 inhibition.
the 2-aminoimidazolopyridine scaffold, which is present in the most potent PA inhibitor so far, can also be used to design hybrid small molecules with a broad anti-Flu spectrum.
the hybrid molecule 36 is a broad anti-Flu small molecule endowed with a potent ability to disrupt the interaction between PA and PB1 subunits.

the hybrid compounds reported in this study are able to inhibit the PA-PB1 complex formation and to inhibit the replication of influenza viruses, thus representing promising candidates to be further developed as anti-influenza drugs.

hybrid molecules, combining the structural features of the most potent compounds identified in previous screenings, may represent a promising strategy to develop novel small molecules able to inhibit the interaction of the PA and PB1 subunits of Flu RNA-dependent RNA polymerases.
